beginner: A good mix combines fast, easy types like radish, broccoli, and arugula with something sweet like pea or sunflower. A couple of rules make it work: soak only the big seeds (pea, sunflower) before sowing, and just mist the sticky ones like basil and cilantro instead of soaking. Different types finish at different times, so many people grow them in separate trays and combine after cutting. Important: never grow microgreens from tomato, pepper, or eggplant seed, as those baby plants are not safe to eat.
seasoned: A balanced mix pairs fast brassicas (radish, broccoli, kale, arugula, mustard) for quick bulk and color with a sweet large-seed type (pea or sunflower, presoaked) and, if you want complexity, a slower aromatic (basil, cilantro). The practical splits are: presoak the large seeds only; mist (never soak) the mucilaginous ones (basil, cilantro, cress, chia); and either sow a pre-blended mix or grow types separately and combine at harvest, since blackout times and finish dates differ. Never use seed from solanaceous crops (tomato, pepper, eggplant), because their seedlings carry alkaloids and are not safe to eat raw.

Dense, even contact is what gives a uniform stand and a clean single cut.

beginner: Microgreens are baby vegetable and herb plants that you harvest very young, about 1 to 3 weeks after planting, when they are just a couple of inches tall. You grow them indoors all year on a shallow tray of seed-starting mix or a special growing mat. The steps are always the same: scatter seeds thickly, cover the tray to keep it dark for a few days while they sprout, then move it into the light to green up, then snip and eat. A mix is just several kinds grown together for variety. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
seasoned: Microgreens are the young seedlings of vegetables and herbs, harvested at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage roughly 1 to 3 weeks after sowing. They are grown indoors year-round in a short repeatable cycle: a dense even sow on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat, a brief dark blackout to drive even germination and stem stretch, then light to green up, then cut. A mix blends several types (fast brassicas, larger soaked seeds, and slower greens) for a range of color and flavor in one tray. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere.

beginner: Your microgreens are ready when the first little seed-leaves are open and, for many types, the first true leaf is just showing, usually 1 to 2 weeks after sowing. seasoned: Cut at the cotyledon to first-true-leaf stage, typically 7 to 21 days from sowing depending on the type (the mix runs about 10 to 14). Snip just above the medium with clean scissors; the stand will not regrow, so the tray is a single cut.
